title: How Indian courts actually apply the polluter pays principle
p1: A company pollutes a river. Who pays for the damage? The surprising answer: it is not always just a fine imposed by the government. Indian courts have often made polluters pay for restoring the environment itself.
p2: Many people think the polluter pays principle means paying a penalty and moving on. But courts have applied it differently. The idea is that the person or organisation causing environmental harm must bear the cost of repairing that harm, not leave society to pay for it.
p3: The Supreme Court has used this principle in cases involving industrial pollution, ordering polluters to fund clean-up measures, compensate affected communities, and take responsibility for environmental restoration. It is less about punishment and more about making the wrongdoer accountable for the real consequences of their actions. A business activity may be legal, but it cannot come at an unfair cost to public health and nature.
conclusion: Do you think companies causing environmental damage should pay only fines, or should they be responsible for complete restoration of the harm they create?
